summary: Describes the protocol elements, semantics and encodings of LDAP, which gives access to distributed directory services following X.500 models. The elements are based on the X.500 Directory Access Protocol. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4511 specifies the LDAP version 3 messages that clients use to access a directory. It defines operations for authentication, searching, adding, changing, and removing directory entries.

subtitle: The LDAP version 3 protocol for searching and changing distributed directory entries.

tldr.problem: Clients need a common protocol to access distributed directories based on X.500 models without using the full Directory Access Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: LDAP defines request and response operations inside an LDAPMessage envelope, encoded with a restricted form of ASN.1 BER over a reliable connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4511 specifies LDAP version 3 protocol elements, meanings, and transfer. It replaces earlier LDAP specifications, including RFC 2251 and RFC 3771.

today: RFC 4511 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. Its text obsoletes RFC 2251 and RFC 3771, plus Sections 2 and 4 of RFC 2830; the unit metadata lists no later update.

sections.title: The LDAP Client and Server Model
sections.content:
A directory user accesses a directory through a client, which communicates with one or more servers. LDAP defines the operations, their meanings, and how the protocol elements are encoded and transferred.

A client sends a request and the server performs the operation and normally returns a response. Operations are generally independent and atomic, and requests and responses need not be synchronous.
sections.plainLanguage: An LDAP client sends a request to a directory server, which performs the operation and returns a result. The protocol supports multiple operations within a session.

sections.title: The LDAP Message Envelope
sections.content:
Every LDAP operation is carried in an LDAPMessage envelope. It includes a message ID, one protocol operation, and optional controls. The message ID connects a response to its request; a request uses a nonzero ID distinct from other requests still in progress.

LDAP strings use UTF-8. Result messages include a result code and may include a matched name, diagnostic text, or referral. Clients must not depend on diagnostic text because its wording is not standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: Each LDAP request and response has an envelope with an ID, so a client can match an answer to a request. Result codes provide the standardized outcome.

sections.title: Starting and Ending a Session
sections.content:
Bind exchanges authentication information and is the LDAP authenticate operation. A request identifies the protocol version, name, and authentication choice: a simple password or a SASL mechanism. This RFC describes version 3 and does not define version negotiation.

After sending Bind, the client waits for the Bind response before sending further LDAP messages. Unbind ends the session; despite its name, it is a quit operation rather than the opposite of authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Bind starts or changes authentication for an LDAP session. Unbind ends the session and does not undo the earlier authentication exchange.

sections.title: Searching a Directory
sections.content:
A Search request sets a starting entry, a scope, limits, a filter, and the attributes to return. The scope can be the starting entry, its immediate children, or the whole subtree. Filters combine tests such as equality, substring, presence, and ordering comparisons.

The server returns zero or more entries and continuation references, followed by one final result. A reference identifies another server that may hold part of the directory. Clients that follow references must avoid loops and support at least ten nested referrals.
sections.plainLanguage: A search specifies where to look, how far to search, which entries match, and which attributes to return. Results may include references to other servers when the directory is distributed.

sections.title: Changing Entries and Extending LDAP
sections.content:
LDAP operations can add, modify, delete, rename, compare, or abandon work on entries. A Modify request applies its changes in order as one atomic operation; if it reports an error, none of the requested changes were applied. Delete applies only to entries with no children.

Controls add semantics to existing operations, while Extended operations define new request and response pairs. An unsupported critical control causes the server to reject the operation; an unsupported noncritical control is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP supports common directory changes and checks. Modifications are applied together, while controls and extended operations provide defined ways to add features.

sections.title: Encoding and Transport
sections.content:
LDAP uses a subset of ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules and a reliable, connection-oriented byte stream. Over TCP, the assigned well-known port is 389, though clients must be able to contact servers on other valid TCP ports.

The StartTLS extended operation can add a TLS layer to an LDAP session. The client must wait for the StartTLS response and complete TLS negotiation before sending other LDAP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP messages use a defined binary encoding and travel over a reliable connection. StartTLS can add a protected TLS connection to an existing session.

sections.title: Authentication and Data Protection
sections.content:
Simple authentication sends a password, so the RFC strongly discourages it when the transport does not provide confidentiality. SASL or TLS can add security services. Servers are encouraged to prevent anonymous clients from modifying directory data.

Referrals can redirect clients to a rogue server, and diagnostic fields can reveal whether data exists. Implementations should protect sensitive results, validate their security state during a session, and handle malformed or unusually long encodings robustly.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords and directory data need a protected transport when confidentiality matters. Clients should also treat referrals carefully because they can redirect a request.
